items.content: ICML 2027 Call For Papers The 44th International Conference on Machine Learning (ICML 2027) will be held in Rio de Janeiro, Brazil, July 31-August 6 , as an in-person event. In addition to the main conference sessions, the conference will include tutorials, workshops and an expo. We invite submissions of papers on original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community for the main conference proceedings. All papers will be reviewed in a double-blind process and accepted papers will be presented at the conference. Papers must be prepared and submitted as a single file: 8 pages for the main paper, with unlimited pages for references, the impact statement, and appendices. There will be no separate deadline for the submission of supplementary material. The final versions of accepted papers will be allowed one extra page for the main paper. Note: ICML is planning to make some updates to the submission process (but not the submission format). We will announce them by late November, please stay tuned. Change in policy: two-stage reviewing process: ICML 2027 will review submissions in two stages. In the first stage, the area chair assigned to each paper decides whether it should proceed to the second stage. Papers that would clearly not be accepted receive a first-stage rejection. Every proposed first-stage reject must be confirmed by a senior area chair, and when in doubt, papers go to full review. Authors of papers that receive a first-stage rejection will be notified by February 23, 2027 with a short justification. All other papers go through the usual review process, and final decisions will be announced on May 3, 2027. This process is similar to the expedited initial review used by many top journals, where an editor or senior reviewer assesses whether a submission is sufficiently competitive to warrant a full round of external review. We recognize that any early-stage review process carries some risk that a good paper could be rejected prematurely. The requirement that every first-stage rejection be reviewed by both an AC and an SAC, together with the principle that papers should proceed to full review whenever there is doubt, is intended to minimize this risk. The goal of this process is to reduce the number of low-quality papers that go through full review. Change in policy: contribution type in submission/reviewing: ICML 2027 asks all authors to select the Contribution Type that best reflects the primary scientific contribution of their submission. The available types are General (most papers) , Theory , Application-driven , Concept and Feasibility , Negative Results , and Datasets, Evaluations and Benchmarks. Contribution types were introduced at NeurIPS 2026. They will be used to help guide reviewing and as one factor in reviewer and Area Chair matching. Authors should select the type that best represents the main contribution of the paper, recognizing that submissions may naturally contain elements of multiple types. Please see the full ICML 2027 Contribution Types Policy and Guidance for detailed descriptions and reviewing expectations. Change in policy: LLM use in Reviewing: ICML 2027 will use a single policy for LLM use in reviewing, corresponding to Policy B of ICML 2026. In short, reviewers may use privacy-compliant LLMs to help understand the paper and related works and to polish their reviews. Delegating judgement and critique of the paper to LLMs is not allowed, and reviewers remain fully responsible for the content of their reviews. A single policy simplifies reviewer assignment and activities permitted under policy B have broad support even among authors/reviewers that chose policy A at ICML 2026 (see the paper ). The findings from ICML 2026 also suggest that effect of policy B on paper outcomes is minimal. Details and precise guidance for the reviewers are given on the LLM policy page . Change in policy: Use of Generative AI by Authors & Disclosure Policy ICML 2027 requires authors to disclose substantive use of generative AI tools in conducting the research or preparing the submission. This includes uses such as research ideation, mathematical reasoning, experimental design, code generation, data analysis, literature synthesis, and substantial manuscript drafting. Routine editorial assistance, such as spelling, grammar, formatting, and minor clarity edits, does not require disclosure. All submissions must include an AI Disclosure Statement. The statement does not count toward the paper page limit. Authors remain fully responsible for the correctness, originality, and integrity of all submitted content, including any material produced with AI assistance. When generative AI is part of the research methodology itself, its use must also be described in the paper with sufficient detail to understand and reproduce the work. Please see the full ICML 2027 Policy on the Use of Generative AI by Authors for requirements, examples, and guidance. Change in policy: Submission caps and reciprocal reviewing policy. Similar to ICLR 2027, ICML 2027 introduces submission quotas and strengthens reciprocal reviewing to cope with the growth in submissions. No author may appear on more than 20 submissions. Each submission must designate one of its authors as reciprocal reviewer, and an author can be designated as the reciprocal reviewer for at most 6 submissions. Each author may appear on at most one submission in which no author is an eligible reciprocal reviewer. Authors with 3 or more submissions must also serve on the program committee, as a reviewer, area chair or senior area chair. Submissions that do not meet these requirements will be desk rejected. Eligibility criteria and further details are given in the guide on Submission Quotas and Reciprocal Reviewing . Please review Author Instructions , an Example Paper , and use the correct Style Files . Submitted papers that do not conform to these policies will be rejected without review. Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): general machine learning (active learning, clustering, online learning, ranking, supervised, semi- and self-supervised learning, time series analysis, etc.) deep learning (architectures, generative models, theory, etc.) evaluation (methodology, meta studies, replicability and validity, human-in-the-loop, etc.) theory of machine learning (statistical learning theory, bandits, game theory, decision theory, etc.) machine learning systems (improved implementation and scalability, hardware, libraries, distributed methods, etc.) optimization (convex and non-convex optimization, matrix/tensor methods, stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.) probabilistic methods (Bayesian methods, graphical models, Monte Carlo methods, etc.) reinforcement learning (decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics, etc.) trustworthy machine learning (reliability, causality, fairness, interpretability, privacy, robustness, safety, etc.) application-driven machine learning (innovative techniques, problems, and datasets that are of interest to the machine learning community and driven by the needs of end-users in applications such as healthcare, physical sciences, biosciences, social sciences, sustainability, and climate etc.) Similar to last year, we also invite submissions of position papers (call for paper is coming soon). Submissions will be handled separately from the main track submissions. Papers published at ICML are indexed in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research through the Journal of Machine Learning Research. We are recruiting reviewers: if you would like to volonteer, please fill this form: Self-nomination form for reviewing Important Dates and Submission Site Submission site opens: January 8, 2027. Suggested OpenReview account creation deadline: January 8, 2027. (If you do not already have an OpenReview account, please register by this date, otherwise we cannot guarantee that your account will be activated in time.**) Abstract submission deadline: January 14, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Full paper submission deadline: January 22, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Abstracts and papers can be submitted through OpenReview: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICML.cc/2027/Conference Note: Position papers should be submitted through a separate OpenReview site, as outlined in the upcoming Call for Position Papers (to be available soon). ** OpenReview: All authors must have an OpenReview account. It is strongly recommended that you sign up for OpenReview (or associate your existing account) with an institutional email. If you sign up for OpenReview with an institutional email, your account will be activated immediately; otherwise it can take up to two weeks for your account to be activated. Policies Optional in-Person Attendance Attendance for authors of accepted papers is optional. After acceptance notifications, the authors will be able to decide by a specified date whether they wish to present their paper in person at the conference or they just wish to include their paper in the proceedings (without presentation at the conference). Regardless of this choice, all the accepted papers will receive equivalent treatment in the proceedings. They will all be eligible for ICML awards as well as for the designations of distinction corresponding to the past “oral presentations” and “spotlight posters.” For proceedings-only papers, at least one of the authors must obtain virtual registration. Deadlines Abstract and paper submission deadlines are strict. In no circumstances will extensions be given. Changes to Abstract/Title/Authorship Authors should include a full title for their paper, complete author list, and complete abstract in the submission form by the abstract submission deadline. While it is possible to edit the title and abstract until the full paper submission deadline, submissions with “placeholder” abstracts that are substantially rewritten for the full submission risk being removed without consideration. The author list cannot be changed after the abstract deadline. After the abstract deadline, authors may be reordered, but not added or removed. Double-Blind Review All submissions must be anonymized and may not contain any information with the intention or consequence of violating the double-blind reviewing policy. Authors are allowed to post versions of their work on preprint servers such as arXiv. They are also allowed to give talks on the work(s) submitted to ICML during the review. However, under no circumstances should the work be advertised as an ICML submission at any time during the review period, i.e., from the time the authors submit the paper to the communication of the accept/reject decisions. If the authors have posted or plan to post a non-anonymized version of the paper online before the ICML decisions are made, the submitted version must not refer to the non-anonymized version. Dual and Concurrent Submission Authors may not submit papers that are identical, or substantially similar, to versions that have been previously published, accepted for publication, or submitted in parallel to other conferences or journals. Such submissions violate our dual submission policy, and the organizers have the right to reject such submissions, or to remove them from the proceedings. Any concurrent ICML submissions with an overlapping set of authors will also be treated as prior work (so, for example, if publishing one would render the other too incremental, then this may be considered grounds for rejection). Note that submissions that have been or are being presented at workshops without published proceedings do not violate the dual-submission policy. Reviewing Criteria Submissions should report original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community. All claims must be clearly stated and supported by reproducible experiments and/or sound theoretical analysis. The contributions must be situated in the context of the broader scientific and machine learning research literature, acknowledging and differentiating from relevant prior works as appropriate. See Reviewer Instructions for more information. Ethical Conduct for Peer Review Authors are expected to follow standard ethical conduct for peer review. In particular: Plagiarism in any form is forbidden. Prompt injection is forbidden. Advertising work (e.g., in a talk, on social media) as being under submission to ICML during the review period is forbidden. Any form of collusion, whether explicit or tacit (e.g., where authors cooperate with reviewers, ACs, or SACs to obtain favorable or unfavorable reviews) is forbidden. If you believe someone may be engaging in unethical conduct, please notify ICML by filling out the Ethics Violation Reporting form . You can also report suspected violations to program-chairs@icml.cc . All suspected unethical behaviors will be investigated by program chairs, integrity chair, or the ICML Oversight Committee, and individuals found violating the rules may face sanctions and/or have their submissions rejected. We will also collect names of individuals who are found to have violated ethics standards; if individuals representing conferences, journals, or other organizations request this list for decision-making purposes, we may make this information available to them. See Peer-review Ethics for additional details. Impact Statements Authors are required to include a statement of the potential broader impact of their work, including its ethical aspects and future societal consequences. This statement should be in a separate section at the end of the paper (co-located with Acknowledgements, before References), and does not count toward the paper page limit. In many cases, where the ethical impacts and expected societal implications are those that are well established when advancing the field of machine learning, substantial discussion is not required, and a simple statement such as: “This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.” The above statement can be used verbatim in such cases, but we encourage authors to think about whether there is content that does warrant further discussion, as this statement will be apparent if the paper is later flagged for ethics review. In particular, Reviewers and ACs may flag submissions for ethics review. Flagged submissions will be sent to an ethics review committee for comments. Ethics reviewers do not have the authority to reject papers, but in extreme cases, papers may be rejected by the program chairs on ethical grounds, regardless of scientific quality or contribution. For tips on writing the impact statement, see this post written for NeurIPS 2020 . Lay Summaries Authors of accepted papers will be required to submit a short “lay summary” of their work (also called "plain language summary") in OpenReview when submitting their camera-ready paper. As machine learning is becoming a more prevalent topic of interest in society, it is important to participate in science communication with the public. See this paper for guidelines. Additional details and examples will be provided prior to the camera-ready deadline. Self-Rankings Continuing the practice introduced at ICML 2026, authors with multiple submissions will be required to provide a self-assessment of the quality of their own submissions through a ranking. Disagreements between author rankings and reviewer scores will be used to flag papers that may warrant additional attention from area chairs and to help guide the assignment of emergency reviewers. Submitted self-rankings will be accessible only to the program chairs, associate program chairs, and integrity chairs. Area chairs will have access only to a coarse measure of disagreement between author rankings and reviewer scores.

Topics of interest include (but are not limited to): general machine learning (active learning, clustering, online learning, ranking, supervised, semi- and self-supervised learning, time series analysis, etc.) deep learning (architectures, generative models, theory, etc.) evaluation (methodology, meta studies, replicability and validity, human-in-the-loop, etc.) theory of machine learning (statistical learning theory, bandits, game theory, decision theory, etc.) machine learning systems (improved implementation and scalability, hardware, libraries, distributed methods, etc.) optimization (convex and non-convex optimization, matrix/tensor methods, stochastic, online, non-smooth, composite, etc.) probabilistic methods (Bayesian methods, graphical models, Monte Carlo methods, etc.) reinforcement learning (decision and control, planning, hierarchical RL, robotics, etc.) trustworthy machine learning (reliability, causality, fairness, interpretability, privacy, robustness, safety, etc.) application-driven machine learning (innovative techniques, problems, and datasets that are of interest to the machine learning community and driven by the needs of end-users in applications such as healthcare, physical sciences, biosciences, social sciences, sustainability, and climate etc.) Similar to last year, we also invite submissions of position papers (call for paper is coming soon). Submissions will be handled separately from the main track submissions. Papers published at ICML are indexed in the Proceedings of Machine Learning Research through the Journal of Machine Learning Research. We are recruiting reviewers: if you would like to volonteer, please fill this form: Self-nomination form for reviewing Important Dates and Submission Site Submission site opens: January 8, 2027. Suggested OpenReview account creation deadline: January 8, 2027. (If you do not already have an OpenReview account, please register by this date, otherwise we cannot guarantee that your account will be activated in time.**) Abstract submission deadline: January 14, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Full paper submission deadline: January 22, 2027 11:59 PM AOE or Abstracts and papers can be submitted through OpenReview: https://openreview.net/group?id=ICML.cc/2027/Conference Note: Position papers should be submitted through a separate OpenReview site, as outlined in the upcoming Call for Position Papers (to be available soon). ** OpenReview: All authors must have an OpenReview account. It is strongly recommended that you sign up for OpenReview (or associate your existing account) with an institutional email. If you sign up for OpenReview with an institutional email, your account will be activated immediately; otherwise it can take up to two weeks for your account to be activated. Policies Optional in-Person Attendance Attendance for authors of accepted papers is optional. After acceptance notifications, the authors will be able to decide by a specified date whether they wish to present their paper in person at the conference or they just wish to include their paper in the proceedings (without presentation at the conference). Regardless of this choice, all the accepted papers will receive equivalent treatment in the proceedings. They will all be eligible for ICML awards as well as for the designations of distinction corresponding to the past “oral presentations” and “spotlight posters.” For proceedings-only papers, at least one of the authors must obtain virtual registration. Deadlines Abstract and paper submission deadlines are strict. In no circumstances will extensions be given. Changes to Abstract/Title/Authorship Authors should include a full title for their paper, complete author list, and complete abstract in the submission form by the abstract submission deadline. While it is possible to edit the title and abstract until the full paper submission deadline, submissions with “placeholder” abstracts that are substantially rewritten for the full submission risk being removed without consideration. The author list cannot be changed after the abstract deadline. After the abstract deadline, authors may be reordered, but not added or removed. Double-Blind Review All submissions must be anonymized and may not contain any information with the intention or consequence of violating the double-blind reviewing policy. Authors are allowed to post versions of their work on preprint servers such as arXiv. They are also allowed to give talks on the work(s) submitted to ICML during the review. However, under no circumstances should the work be advertised as an ICML submission at any time during the review period, i.e., from the time the authors submit the paper to the communication of the accept/reject decisions. If the authors have posted or plan to post a non-anonymized version of the paper online before the ICML decisions are made, the submitted version must not refer to the non-anonymized version. Dual and Concurrent Submission Authors may not submit papers that are identical, or substantially similar, to versions that have been previously published, accepted for publication, or submitted in parallel to other conferences or journals. Such submissions violate our dual submission policy, and the organizers have the right to reject such submissions, or to remove them from the proceedings. Any concurrent ICML submissions with an overlapping set of authors will also be treated as prior work (so, for example, if publishing one would render the other too incremental, then this may be considered grounds for rejection). Note that submissions that have been or are being presented at workshops without published proceedings do not violate the dual-submission policy. Reviewing Criteria Submissions should report original and rigorous research of significant interest to the machine learning community. All claims must be clearly stated and supported by reproducible experiments and/or sound theoretical analysis. The contributions must be situated in the context of the broader scientific and machine learning research literature, acknowledging and differentiating from relevant prior works as appropriate. See Reviewer Instructions for more information. Ethical Conduct for Peer Review Authors are expected to follow standard ethical conduct for peer review. In particular: Plagiarism in any form is forbidden. Prompt injection is forbidden. Advertising work (e.g., in a talk, on social media) as being under submission to ICML during the review period is forbidden. Any form of collusion, whether explicit or tacit (e.g., where authors cooperate with reviewers, ACs, or SACs to obtain favorable or unfavorable reviews) is forbidden. If you believe someone may be engaging in unethical conduct, please notify ICML by filling out the Ethics Violation Reporting form . You can also report suspected violations to program-chairs@icml.cc . All suspected unethical behaviors will be investigated by program chairs, integrity chair, or the ICML Oversight Committee, and individuals found violating the rules may face sanctions and/or have their submissions rejected. We will also collect names of individuals who are found to have violated ethics standards; if individuals representing conferences, journals, or other organizations request this list for decision-making purposes, we may make this information available to them. See Peer-review Ethics for additional details. Impact Statements Authors are required to include a statement of the potential broader impact of their work, including its ethical aspects and future societal consequences. This statement should be in a separate section at the end of the paper (co-located with Acknowledgements, before References), and does not count toward the paper page limit. In many cases, where the ethical impacts and expected societal implications are those that are well established when advancing the field of machine learning, substantial discussion is not required, and a simple statement such as: “This paper presents work whose goal is to advance the field of machine learning. There are many potential societal consequences of our work, none of which we feel must be specifically highlighted here.” The above statement can be used verbatim in such cases, but we encourage authors to think about whether there is content that does warrant further discussion, as this statement will be apparent if the paper is later flagged for ethics review. In particular, Reviewers and ACs may flag submissions for ethics review. Flagged submissions will be sent to an ethics review committee for comments. Ethics reviewers do not have the authority to reject papers, but in extreme cases, papers may be rejected by the program chairs on ethical grounds, regardless of scientific quality or contribution. For tips on writing the impact statement, see this post written for NeurIPS 2020 . Lay Summaries Authors of accepted papers will be required to submit a short “lay summary” of their work (also called "plain language summary") in OpenReview when submitting their camera-ready paper. As machine learning is becoming a more prevalent topic of interest in society, it is important to participate in science communication with the public. See this paper for guidelines. Additional details and examples will be provided prior to the camera-ready deadline. Self-Rankings Continuing the practice introduced at ICML 2026, authors with multiple submissions will be required to provide a self-assessment of the quality of their own submissions through a ranking. Disagreements between author rankings and reviewer scores will be used to flag papers that may warrant additional attention from area chairs and to help guide the assignment of emergency reviewers. Submitted self-rankings will be accessible only to the program chairs, associate program chairs, and integrity chairs. Area chairs will have access only to a coarse measure of disagreement between author rankings and reviewer scores.

items.title: Flint-interactive: A language for creating interactive data visualizations
items.summary: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports
items.content: At a glance Brings rich interactivity to AI-generated charts: Flint-interactive enables agents to create data visualizations that users can explore directly through clicking, filtering, zooming, highlighting, and cross-chart interactions. Makes complex interactions easier to build: Instead of requiring low-level visualization code, Flint-interactive lets users and agents define behaviors using high-level semantic events and update operators. Improves reliability and reduces development effort: By using Flint’s compiler to handle interaction logic and visual dependencies, the system helps avoid many of the layout, rendering, and debugging challenges common in custom interactive visualizations. Connects charts, text, tables, and applications: Flint-interactive supports interactive data stories, dashboards, and connected experiences where actions in one view can update charts, documents, widgets, or application state in another. AI agents make it easy to analyze data and generate reports with data visualizations. They help users examine patterns more efficiently than by reading verbose text. However, when we’re feeling exploratory, we want to go beyond static visualizations. : We want to interact with charts to zoom in on details, compare data across charts, or even highlight related text in the document from a chart selection, and vice versa. This requires agents to be able to create interactive data visualizations that communicate information while letting readers explore beyond the author’s chosen view, ideally with the quality of interactive stories in sophisticated data journalism. This leaves us wondering: (As a user) Can I interact with charts directly in chat to explore the data and ask follow-up questions based on what I select? (As a developer) Can I enable the AI agents I build for my customers to generate interactive visualizations that help them explore and understand their data? Yes, it’s possible, but there is a significant practical gap. Even with capable frontier models, we still face: High generation cost. Agents rarely produce a fully satisfactory interactive visualization in one turn. Repeated rounds of reasoning, coding, and debugging consume tokens and time. Reliability. Interactive visualizations are challenging enough that expressive interactive charts introduce poor layouts or broken interactions easily, and we risk introducing new problems when trying to fix them. These challenges help explain why consistently generating high-quality interactive visualizations remain difficult in real-world use. Meanwhile, built-in interactions in some visualization libraries are not expressive enough on their own to create bespoke interactive charts. And these challenges are results of the lack of an expressive yet high-level language to specify visual interactions. Foundry Labs Foundry Labs bridges the distance between Microsoft breakthroughs and the builders, scientists, and curious minds who can put them to work. Foundry Labs Opens in a new tab Flint-interactive Flint-interactive (opens in new tab) is a language for creating interactive data visualizations on top of Flint. It allows users to create dashboards, data stories, and interactive artifacts more easily. The power of Flint-interactive comes from Flint’s compiler, which translates user interactions into semantic events that capture the meaning behind what users select. It then uses high-level operators to update visualizations in response to those events, making sophisticated interactions far easier to create and maintain. This shifts the heavy burden of resolving complex dependencies between interaction and visual logic to the compiler, so the user (or the agent) can easily describe expressive interactions with high-level specifications. Example 1: We can enable the user to brush one visual view, and the chart highlights all groups of country selected by the user with a simple preset interaction linked-brush. How to use 1. Use Flint in your chat Use Flint Interactive directly in your chat or canvas environment through Flint-MCP and MCP Apps, following the MCP setup guide. With the latest release, tell your agent what to chart and which interactions you want; it can generate an interaction_spec alongside the Flint chart spec and render the interactive chart in your conversation. Example 2: Using Flint-interactive in the chat environment, allowing the agent to produce interactive charts more reliably with simple Flint specifications. It also enables the user to select and pass context to the follow-up turns. 2. Build an interactive app with Flint Build interactive charts in a dashboard, data story, or other application with Flint Interactive Canvas. Your app can use event handlers to process semantic events emitted by Flint Canvas, for example to filter a table, update another chart, or change application state. To let your app’s widgets control how the chart updates, send update operators to Flint Canvas. Example 2: Flint-interactive allows developers to define interactions between charts and external elements (e.g., table, paragraph). Here, the user can click the table to highlight points in the chart and verse versa. 3. Create bespoke interactions To create bespoke interactions beyond Flint’s presets, define a trigger and a custom handle function with the programming API that maps semantic events to custom chart update sequences. For example, a handler can highlight a clicked country and label it by name. It combines set-style and set-annotation without manipulating renderer-specific marks. Example 4: The agent can create bespoke interactive visualizations with Flint’s programming API. In this DimpVis example, the user can drag the point along the time path to visualize how all cities’ temperature and precipitation changes. How it works Flint Canvas is a state machine that tracks user interactions on the canvas and manages visual rendering state. Flint makes interaction specification easy by separating visual logic, managed by the compiler, from interaction logic, specified by the user at the semantic level: Visual logic: The compiler automatically resolves raw triggers, such as clicks, drags, and key presses, into semantic events that identify chart elements and data. It also translates update operators into rendered canvas changes, handling hit testing, and low-level visual updates. Interaction logic: The user specifies interactions by mapping semantic interaction events to chart update operators, such as set style to highlight data, set annotation to label a point, or set viewport to pan or zoom. The user can also use those semantic events to update external tables, widgets, or application states. Figure 1: Flint interactive allows the agent to describe interaction logic by mapping “what semantic event is the user interacting with” to “what updates they want for the canvas surface”. The compiler takes the heavy lifting of resolving visual updates and manages the runtime, which makes interaction authoring more reliable c and cost effective. This separation means users do not need to reverse-engineer rendering logic or manipulate renderer-specific marks, making interactions easier to specify and maintain. Furthermore, because event generation and visual updates are compositional, the same model also connects Flint with tables, text, other charts, and widgets to build interactive stories and dashboards. Try it now! Video playback requires cookie consent Chart users: Set up Flint in your chat (opens in new tab) and ask your agent to create an interactive chart. Find inspiration in the interaction gallery. App builders: Build interactive dashboards, data stories, and connected views with the programming API (opens in new tab) . Share the interaction-author skill with your coding agent to add presets to your app. Interaction designers: Explore the bespoke examples (opens in new tab) , design a new interaction, and turn it into a reusable preset. Propose a preset on GitHub and share your prototype or implementation to help expand Flint’s interaction vocabulary. items.content: At a glance Formal methods for everyday software. PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. Only admin accounts get admin tokens. We kept the request rough on purpose. Capturing the intent of the user and turning the user request into something a proof can check is PDD Kit’s job. Step 1: Questions before code PDD Kit’s planning workflow, pdd-plan, reads the code and comes back, before writing anything, with questions in a Decisions tab. When a question depends on how the code works, the card explains that part first: the goal, how the pieces fit, and the exact function involved, so you can answer without opening the source. Figure 2. The first decision card. “Only with the right password” on its own is also met by a login that refuses everyone. Proving both ways rules that out. The question looks pedantic, but it matters. “You only get a token with the right password” rules out the bad case, a wrong password getting a token, and a login that refuses everyone keeps that promise perfectly. “The right password always works” is the half that rules it out. Formally, the first is an implication (token ⇒ right password) and the second is its converse. Together they make an “if and only if.” An agent left alone would pick one without telling you, but here the developer picked both ways. It includes a flowchart of the login being specified, a spec landscape of what will be proved and what will be trusted, and, when a picture helps, a mental model. For login, PDD Kit drew a ticket desk (Figure 3). Figure 3. PDD Kit’s mental model for login. The field you send picks the window, the window picks the table and with it the role, and nothing prints until the password matches. Below it, the intent map ties each requirement back to the developer’s own words and records how it was settled (Figure 4). Each entry links to the section of the formal spec that models it and to the tests that cover it, and the spec section shows snippets of the Verus contract, annotated so the developer can see how the formal spec models their intent. Figure 4. An intent map entry after the decision: a login gets a token only with the right password for that account, and always with it. The flowchart shows every way the password check can end. The decision card in Figure 2 is the kind of ambiguity an agent would otherwise settle silently. Figure 5 shows how small the difference looks on paper: the two readings disagree in a single cell, a right password that gets no token. Figure 5. Two readings of the same sentence. They differ in one cell, and that cell changes what the proof has to establish. Its first draft proved the decision at the center of login, picking the table and gating on the password, and kept the handler around it trusted and tested. That’s a sensible default, and it’s what PDD Kit recommended, but the developer wanted more. The handler is where the lookups get awaited and the token gets signed, and that glue is exactly where a refactor can quietly swap two lines. So at intent review the developer chose to give the login handler its own async spec, so the proof covers that glue too instead of trusting it (Figure 6). Figure 6. Proving more of login means trusting more small wrappers. The card says so before the developer chooses. That choice moved almost everything into the proof and left the login handler with nothing to do but unpack the request. A new async function, login_flow , carries the contract from the request’s fields all the way to the token or the HTTP error. PDD Kit then brought the revised plan back for a fresh sign-off, because matching your intent isn’t proof, and it doesn’t approve new trust or a wider scope. Step 4: Where proof stops There are plenty of things you can’t prove about a program, and login runs into most of them: Code the verifier can’t see. bcrypt’s hashing, sqlx’s queries and jsonwebtoken’s signing live in other crates, outside the proof. Facts about the outside world. What SQLite holds right now and what time the clock says are inputs to the program, not something its code can establish. Whether, and how fast, something finishes. The spec says what you get if login answers. A hung query, or a slow one, breaks nothing in it. Anything a person has to judge , like whether an error message helps or a screen makes sense. Whatever nobody wrote down. A proof covers its spec and says nothing about requirements outside it. That’s where empirical verification comes in. PDD Kit spells out the trusted boundary, the part of the TCB this proof leans on. It wraps each trusted piece in a small function with an assumed contract, using Verus’s #[verifier::external_body] or external_fn_specification , asks the developer to accept each one on its own, and writes a test for every assumed clause into the plan. For login, the developer signed off on six pieces: The two lookups, Customer::find_by_email and Admin::find_by_username . Each awaited, successful lookup returns exactly the row its own table holds for that email or username, or none. check_password , a thin wrapper around bcrypt::verify . It errors only on a stored hash bcrypt can’t read, and Ok(true) means exactly the right password. generate_token , which signs exactly the claims it is given under the configured secret and reports a signing failure as a 500. expiry_from_now , which reads the clock and writes an expiry exactly 24 hours later. database_error , which turns a failed lookup into today’s 500 with sqlx’s message. The login handler shell, which unpacks the request and passes its fields to login_flow unchanged. In the spec, a lookup keeps its code where it is and gets a contract from the outside with external_fn_specification : /// Looks up a customer by exact email. /// Trusted, not proved: the SQL query runs in sqlx, which Verus cannot check. /// Every customer promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_fn_specification] pub async fn ex_customer_find_by_email(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, email: &str) -> (r: Result , sqlx::Error>) ensures // When the query succeeds, it returns the customers row on // file for exactly this email, or None when there is none. r matches Ok(found) ==> found == customer_on_file(email@), { Customer::find_by_email(pool, email).await } The clock is a small wrapper marked #[verifier::external_body] . Verus uses its ensures clause and never reads the body: /// Reads the clock and computes a token's expiry 24 hours ahead. /// Trusted, not proved: chrono's clock is outside the proof. /// It panics if the time is out of range, as today's login does; /// that panic is not promised against. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn expiry_from_now() -> (r: Expiry) ensures // The expiry is exactly 24 hours (86,400 seconds) after the clock reading. r.exp as int == r.now as int + 86_400, { ... } Figure 7 puts the three layers together: what Verus proves, what people accept and tests check, and what nobody is promising. Figure 7. Where the login proof stops. Verus proves the core for every input. People accept the trusted ring and tests check it. The plan lists what nobody is promising. Figure 8 maps what gets proved and what gets trusted. Each trust decision is its own card. It shows the clauses Verus will take on faith, what the developer is accepting, and which promise falls apart if the assumption is wrong (Figure 9). Every assumed clause then gets an empirical check in the plan’s Empirical verification section, written as Given/When/Then scenarios before any test exists (Figure 10). An entry says planned until it has run, and then it records the command’s result and the commit it ran against. Figure 8. What gets proved and what gets trusted in login. Green functions are proved by Verus for every input. Amber pieces are trusted, accepted by the developer, and checked by the planned tests in the plan’s §4.1. Figure 9. A trust card for check_password . Verus takes these two clauses on faith, so a person accepts them and two tests check them. Figure 10. A planned test for the trusted check_password , written before the test exists. The plan labels a passing test as evidence rather than proof. The plan is just as explicit about what nobody is promising: that the login future ever completes, that an out-of-range clock won’t panic, anything about the timing or rate of attempts, and how other endpoints read the role. You might be wondering whether someone now has to read the proof instead of the code. Nobody does, because the coding agent writes the proof and Verus checks every step of it. If Verus accepts the proof, it holds whether or not anyone reads it. The spec is what the proof is held to, so that’s what people review, and this one is short enough to learn to read in a few minutes. Each function gets an ensures block: statements about its result, r, that must hold for every possible input. Verus checks them when you build, and if any clause could fail for even one input, the build fails and Verus points at that clause. Each clause reads as an if-then, and Figure 11 takes apart the clause for the developer’s first requirement. Figure 11. The ensures clause on login_flow for “You only get a token with the right password.” The same account a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. Notice that the same a appears on every line, which ties the password check to the token. For example, imagine a bug where login checks the password against one account but signs the token for another. Bob logs in with his own, correct password and gets back a token for Alice’s account. Each step looks fine on its own, but this clause catches it, because the password check and the token have to name the same account. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you await it. No

PDD Kit helps you turn your intent into a formal spec, then proves the code your agent writes for every input and uses tests where a proof can’t reach. It takes formal methods beyond niche, specialist work to engineers without a formal methods background and to everyday applications, like the full-stack web app shown here. Exhaustive line-by-line human review can become difficult to scale as AI agents generate increasingly large amounts of code. The plan is supposed to be the contract between you and a coding agent, but nothing actually forces the agent to follow it. The tests it writes usually check what it built, rather than what you asked for. PDD Kit makes the agent keep the plan. It works with you to turn your intent into a formal specification in Verus (opens in new tab) , proves the agent’s code meets that spec for every input, and falls back to tests where a proof can’t reach. We tried it on a full-stack web app. Inside GitHub Next’s Chopin (opens in new tab) , we used PDD Kit to formally verify the login logic of Pet Store, a Rust (opens in new tab) storefront. Verus hardened the code and uncovered existing bugs, proving the absence of login bugs with respect to the specification. The developer reviewed the intent and never read the generated code line-by-line. The plan is the contract the agent should follow, but nothing constrains the agent to follow it. Coding agents now ship whole features in one sitting often spanning tens of thousands or hundreds of thousands of lines of code. As a result, reading every line of the pull request doesn’t scale to this new way of work. Now, most teams invest in the plan and relevant testing instead: describe to an agent what they want, go back and forth until the plan and proposed tests look right, and hand them off to the agent for implementation. This plan or natural language spec is meant to be the contract that an agent holds. However, in practice, the agent can drift from it. It implements something slightly different, then writes tests that pass for its implementation rather than the code you intended it to write. Continuous integration (CI) grows due to a profusion of low quality and high quantity of tests, coverage looks healthy, and the gap between what you asked for and what shipped stays hidden until a bug report or a nasty edge case shows up. So, how do you reliably scale review as agents generate increasingly large amounts of code? Agent code fails in two ways a careful reviewer would usually catch: it leaves out something obviously necessary, or it does something obviously wrong. Tests alone don’t close that gap, because they only exercise a tiny slice of what a program can do. Closing it needs a different kind of machinery, which is where proofs come in. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab Review asks “does this look right?” A proof answers “is this right?” A mathematical proof shows that code meets its specification for every input, including the ones your test suite can miss. That provides stronger assurance for specified properties than testing alone, especially when line-by-line review isn’t practical. Proofs used to be too expensive for everyday software. You needed specialists, unfamiliar languages, proofs many times larger than the code, and proofs took years to develop, but two things have changed since. First, recent advances in coding agents have made it increasingly practical for them to help generate formal proofs from well-defined specs. Secondly, agents can now better help you write formal specs. We call this new software development paradigm Proof-Driven Development (PDD). PDD Kit is our toolkit for it. How PDD Kit works PDD Kit is to formal methods roughly what Spec Kit (opens in new tab) is to Spec-Driven Development. It runs as a partner inside Chopin (opens in new tab) , GitHub Next’s real-time, multiplayer planning environment, where a team and agents can plan in one shared document. The workflow has two halves (Figure 1). First, team members review intent in plain language. PDD Kit asks the questions a careful reviewer would ask, explains the relevant code as it goes, and records the answers in an intent artifact , a document that bridges the user’s intent with the formal specification or tests. The parts of the user’s intent that can be formalized are converted into formal specifications and the rest, which must be taken on trust, are converted to informal specifications for tests. PDD Kit automatically generates proofs that the code satisfies the derived formal specs and high-quality tests for the informal specs. You don’t need a formal methods background for any of it. Figure 1. Proof-Driven Development with PDD Kit. Team members settle intent. Verus and the test suite hold the code to it. Consequently, every result in PDD Kit says which kind of verification it rests on: Formal verification is a mathematical proof that code satisfies its specification for every possible input, checked by a tool called a verifier. For PDD Kit today, that verifier is Verus (opens in new tab) , a proof language for Rust co-developed by Microsoft Research, Carnegie Mellon University, VMware Research, ETH Zurich, MPI-SWS, UNSW Sydney, the University of Texas at Austin, the University of Michigan, the University of British Columbia, the University of Wisconsin–Madison and the Weizmann Institute of Science. Empirical verification checks code by running it and observing what it does. It covers what a proof can’t reach, such as a third-party cryptography library or a user interface. It uses unit and end-to-end tests, terminal automation, browser agents, and computer-use agents for anything a browser can’t drive. A passing test only shows the code worked on the inputs it tried, so PDD Kit labels it as evidence rather than proof. The line between the two is the Trusted Computing Base (TCB) : the code that the proof assumes behaves as described. PDD Kit makes that line explicit and asks you to sign off on each piece. The capstone: a full-stack web app To show PDD Kit integrating with existing codebases, we built Pet Store, a full-stack web app written entirely in Rust (opens in new tab) . The backend uses Axum (opens in new tab) and SQLite (opens in new tab) and handles inventory, promotions, orders and checkout. The storefront is a Leptos (opens in new tab) app compiled to WebAssembly (opens in new tab) . Together they come to about 5,000 lines of Rust. For brevity in this blog, we focus on formally verifying the login logic of the app, but the same process can be used to verify functional correctness of the entire app. PDD Kit recommends starting with the most sensitive parts of your application and incrementally verifying your application. A login bug can hand an attacker a customer’s account or an admin’s controls, so that’s where proof effort pays off first. The developer’s whole request in Chopin was two sentences: Verify the login logic in backend/src/handlers/auth.rs. Here are my requirements: You only get a token with the right password. The proof says “whatever the database holds, login does the right thing with it,” and a trusted contract says “the lookup returns what the database holds.” /// The customers row the database holds for /// exactly this email, if any, when login looks. /// Left abstract: only `Customer::find_by_email`'s /// trusted contract says what it is. pub uninterp spec fn customer_on_file(email: Seq ) -> Option ; ... /// What bcrypt says about `password` against a /// stored `hash`: Some(true) when it is the password /// the hash was made from, Some(false) when it is /// not, None when bcrypt cannot read the hash. /// Left abstract: its meaning is bcrypt's, taken on trust through `check_password`. pub uninterp spec fn bcrypt_verdict(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> Option ; /// The password is the right one for the stored hash, by bcrypt's verdict. pub open spec fn password_matches(password: Seq , hash: Seq ) -> bool { bcrypt_verdict(password, hash) == Some(true) } On top of those, named_account(email, username) says which account a login names: the customers row for the email when one is sent, otherwise the admins row for the username, otherwise none. It’s written like Rust, but it’s a mathematical definition that never runs and only appears in contracts. Code like this is called ghost code , since the verifier checks it but the compiler erases it from the program. With it, the developer’s two-sentence request ends up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow (Figure 12). /// The account a login names: the customers row for /// the email when one is sent (role "customer"), /// otherwise the admins row for the username (role "admin"), otherwise none. pub open spec fn named_account(email: Option , username: Option ) -> Option { match email { Some(e) => match customer_on_file(e@) { Some(c) => Some(NamedAccount { id: c.id@, password_hash: c.password_hash@, role: customer_role() }), None => None, }, None => match username { Some(u) => match admin_on_file(u@) { Some(a) => Some(NamedAccount { id: a.id@, password_hash: a.password_hash@, role: admin_role() }), None => None, }, None => None, }, } } Figure 12. The two-sentence request and the Both ways decision ended up as eight ensures clauses on login_flow. Four of them keep today’s refusals, so the storefront and the existing API tests keep working. Here’s the whole contract, with its doc comment trimmed. Each clause has the plain-English comment above it that the intent artifact shows the team: /// The whole login, awaited end to end: from the /// request's fields to the token or the HTTP error. /// ... pub async fn login_flow(pool: &sqlx::SqlitePool, config: &Config, email: Option , username: Option , password: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // Neither an email nor a username: 400 with today's message. email is None && username is None ==> (r matches Err(AppError::BadRequest(m)) && m@ == missing_identity_text()), // A token only for the account the login names, with its right // password; it carries that account's id and its table's role. r matches Ok(t) ==> (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.sub@ == a.id && c.role@ == a.role), // The right password for the named account always gets a // token, unless a lookup or signing failure gives 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && password_matches(password@, a.password_hash)) ==> (r is Ok || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A login naming an account nobody holds gets // 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. ((email is Some || username is Some) && named_account(email, username) is None) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // A wrong password for an account whose hash bcrypt // can read gets 401, unless the lookup fails with 500. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) == Some(false)) ==> (r matches Err(AppError::Unauthorized) || r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_))), // An account whose stored hash bcrypt cannot read gets 500 and no token. (named_account(email, username) matches Some(a) && bcrypt_verdict(password@, a.password_hash) is None) ==> r matches Err(AppError::Internal(_)), // The admin role only for an admins row // found by username, with no email sent. (r matches Ok(t) && token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == admin_role()) ==> (email is None && username matches Some(u) && admin_on_file(u@) is Some), // An email login's token always carries the customer role. (r matches Ok(t) && email is Some) ==> (token_claims(t@, config.jwt_secret@) matches Some(c) && c.role@ == customer_role()), { unimplemented!() } The trusted boundary shows up in the code too. check_password is one of the functions whose body Verus doesn’t check. Its contract ties it to bcrypt_verdict , an uninterpreted model of bcrypt with no axioms: /// Asks bcrypt whether `password` matches the stored `hash`. /// Trusted, not proved: Verus cannot check bcrypt's hashing, /// so this wrapper's contract is assumed. /// Every password promise of `login_flow` rests on it. #[verifier::external_body] pub fn check_password(password: &str, hash: &str) -> (r: Result ) ensures // bcrypt answers (Ok) exactly when it can read the stored hash. r is Ok <==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) is Some, // Its answer is its verdict: true for the // right password, false for any other. r matches Ok(b) ==> bcrypt_verdict(password@, hash@) == Some(b), { bcrypt::verify(password, hash).map_err(|e| e.to_string()) } The doc comment above it says what rests on it: every password promise of login_flow . Every login ends in one of a handful of places, and only one of them has a token (Figure 13). The proof covers all of them at once. Figure 13. Every way a login can end, from the plan. login_flow is async: it awaits a database query. Verus can put contracts on async functions, with one rule worth knowing (Figure 14). requires is checked when the call creates the future. ensures describes the value you get when you await it. No

items.content: Microsoft researcher and collaborator combine new mathematical ideas with human-directed AI to resolve a central problem in high-dimensional geometry and probability At a glance Fundamental scientific breakthrough: Researchers resolved the Kannan-Lovász-Simonovits (KLS) conjecture, a 31-year-old problem widely regarded as one of the central open questions in high-dimensional geometry, with implications for statistics, optimization, algorithms, and computer science. A universal geometric principle: The result establishes a universal geometric principle for log-concave distributions, showing that simple flat cuts can capture their narrowest bottlenecks within a fixed factor, regardless of dimension. Human-AI collaboration: The breakthrough emerged from a human-directed agentic research process in which AI systems explored mathematical possibilities while researchers evaluated, pruned, and redirected the search. Independent confirmation: Multiple independent researchers have validated this research, identifying its central criterion as the key breakthrough, followed by a machine-checked formal verification. For decades, a fundamental question about the difficulty of computing in high-dimensional spaces has resisted proof. New research resolves this question, removing a major theoretical obstacle to understanding the efficiency of randomized algorithms used across science and computing. The Kannan–Lovász–Simonovits (KLS) conjecture was proposed in 1995. It asks whether, for a broad class of high-dimensional probability distributions, the best flat or hyperplane cut is always nearly as effective as the best cut of any shape. More precisely, KLS predicts that the two differ by no more than a universal constant, regardless of the number of dimensions. This would establish a dimension-free geometric principle with important consequences for high-dimensional geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. Because the geometry of these cuts governs how quickly random walks can explore a distribution, KLS also plays a central role in the theory of high-dimensional sampling. Figure 1: An illustration of the KLS Conjecture (simplified) on regular tetrahedron. Since 1995, mathematicians have accumulated evidence that the conjecture was true, but a complete proof remained elusive. Now, two researchers, including Xinzhi Zhang from the Machine Learning and Optimization group at Microsoft Research, have proved the KLS conjecture (opens in new tab) . They have shown that the relationship holds with a fixed bound, regardless of how many dimensions a shape has. Before this work, the best known result (opens in new tab) , established in July 2026, allowed that bound to grow slowly as the number of dimensions increased. This work establishes a fundamental geometric principle: high-dimensional spaces are better behaved than previously known, and the obstacles to navigating them do not grow without bound as dimensions increase. Spotlight: Event Series Microsoft Research Forum Join us for a continuous exchange of ideas about research in the era of general AI. Watch the latest episodes on demand. Watch on-demand Opens in a new tab The importance of the KLS conjecture was recognized across the field long before it was resolved. In its 2017-18 Annual Report, the Mathematical Sciences Research Institute (MSRI) (opens in new tab) called it “a central open problem in high-dimensional convex geometry.” The Simons Institute (opens in new tab) described it as “one of the most important open problems in convex geometry.” In the proceedings of the 2022 International Congress of Mathematicians (ICM) (opens in new tab) , Ronen Eldan noted its broad implications for high-dimensional convex and computational geometry. Quanta Magazine (opens in new tab) wrote that KLS “lies at the heart of many questions in statistics and computer science.” Technical details The authors began by improving the July 2026 result in order to make the mathematical bound more precise. Working with AI agents in a structured, human-directed process, they explored more than 100 candidate approaches, many involving lengthy calculations with higher-order tensors. This produced a new mathematical criterion that became the foundation of the final proof. The authors then discovered that the new criterion could be applied recursively. Each improved bound could be fed back into the same argument to produce a still tighter one. In the October 1, 2026 version of the paper, this reduced the dependence on dimension to the iterated logarithm. This function grows extraordinarily slowly, but it still grows with the dimension and therefore did not yet fully resolve the conjecture. The final step was to repeat the entire recursive refinement, rather than applying it only once. This idea was inspired by the authors’ earlier work on fast algorithms for linear programming. The authors proved that the small errors introduced at each stage shrink fast enough that their total remains bounded by a universal constant, independent of the dimension. This eliminated the dependence on the number of dimensions and completed the proof in the October 4, 2026 version of the paper. The recursive method, its repeated application, and the proof that the accumulated errors remain bounded are original contributions of the researchers. AI tools helped explore candidate approaches, carry out detailed derivations, prepare the manuscript, and perform internal proof checks. The researchers determined the mathematical direction, selected the promising ideas, assembled them into the final argument, and verified the proof. Independent confirmation On the same day that the authors posted their complete proof, a separate group of leading experts posted a full proof (opens in new tab) that they developed in parallel. Their work built upon the findings in the first version (opens in new tab) of the Microsoft paper, calling it “the crucial step in the proof.” A third proof (opens in new tab) which appeared separately on the same day relies on a closely related idea. In addition, a Lean 4 formalization (opens in new tab) was subsequently released, combining the key criterion from the first Microsoft paper with additional research. Independent proofs are among mathematics’ strongest forms of validation because they demonstrate that a result does not rest on a single chain of reasoning. The subsequent appearance of alternative approaches and formal verification further strengthens confidence that the field has uncovered a genuine underlying principle rather than a fragile technical argument. The authors have also shortened their proof and verified the streamlined argument in Lean; they plan to release both after final review. Together, these developments provide complementary forms of confirmation. Human-AI guidance In the process of proving KLS, this research also demonstrates the power of having researchers direct AI rather than simply asking AI to solve a complex problem through a single end-to-end run of a frontier model or agent. The authors used an agentic search process with iterative, human-assisted “pruning”: As multiple agents explored variations of an idea in parallel, the researcher examined their intermediate result, eliminated unpromising directions, and passed the most promising result to the next round. Roughly one hundred research trajectories were explored before the key breakthrough emerged. In a separate track of the project, the authors made repeated unguided attempts to solve the same problem with several leading AI models, using roughly the same total token budget as the main process. That effort fell short of the goal. The eventual success depended on both the capabilities of the AI systems and the mathematical judgment of the researchers. Conclusion Taken together, resolving KLS settles a central problem in high-dimensional geometry. A wide range of results that previously relied on the conjecture as an assumption can now be stated unconditionally. The proof therefore provides a stronger foundation for research in convex geometry, probability, and theoretical computer science. The work also demonstrates how carefully guided human-AI collaboration can contribute to genuine scientific discovery while reinforcing, rather than replacing human insight. It highlights the continuing importance of scientific judgment in identifying promising directions, recognizing conceptual connections, and seeing when a partial insight points toward a deeper result. The authors are now simplifying the proof and extending its formal verification so that the mathematics and theoretical computer science communities can more easily examine the result and build on it. Acknowledgements Thank you to our co-author Zhao Song for his contributions to this work, and Victor Reis (opens in new tab) and Ishai Menache for helpful discussions throughout the project. items.content: Back to Articles Granite Switch 4.1.1 — Update models like you update software Enterprise Article Published October 29, 2026 Upvote 36 +30 Kate Soule katesoule Follow ibm-granite Luis A Lastras GrizleeBer Follow ibm-granite Subhajit Chaudhury subhajit1412 Follow ibm-granite Abraham Daniels abedaniels Follow ibm-granite Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1 , showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint. Granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood. Updated Granite Speech ASR model — multilingual speech-to-text across 10 languages with native punctuation and capitalization, so transcripts are ready for downstream models without a formatting pass. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo. Updated Decision adapter in granitelib-core — featuring improved overall performance on the Jev Decision Index test set. While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this update. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy. This pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon. Until then, test out our latest models , and try out the new multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.
